author: Edward O. Wilson
introFa: کتاب «The Social Conquest of Earth» نوشته Edward O. Wilson یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Social Conquest of Earth»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: SOCIAL POLICY & ADMINISTRATION ISSN 0144-5596 VOL. 29, No. 4, DECEMBER 1995, PP. 335-344 Social Justice and the Reform o f Social Security Dorothy J. Wilson and Thomas Wilson Abstract There have been massive increases over the years in expenditure on the public services loosely grouped together as the “weEfare state”, but widespread dissatisfaction persists. This article is a critique of the proposals for reform presented in the Report o f the Commission on Social Justice, set up ty the late John Smith. The report contains a sweeping condemnation of existing arrangements and puts forward a series of recommendations ranging from the health service to decentralization in government and from employment policy to benejits for the elderly. As was perhaps inevitable, some are more precisely presented than others. An important example of the more fully specijiedproposals is one to establish what would, in effect, be a means-tested ‘yension guarantee” but with “means ”so defined as to exclude capital and with much improved “disregards”. Another is the endorsement of the proposals to extend social insurance to part-time workers-a proposal which raises some controversial issues. There is much in this report that deserves close attention, and it is, therefore, all the more unfortunate that its proposals are notpresented in the form of a quantijiedplan for socialpolicy. Even for thejrstjveyears orso of thefifieen the Commission has in mind, there is no attempt at quantijication. The importance of economic growth is rightly stressed, but ‘tfastergrowth ” can become a panacea that obscures the need for choice, not only between private and public expenditure but also between the various components of public policy itsew Keywords UK, Pensions guarantee, Social Justice I The Case for Change Crisis is the chronic condition of the welfare state with complaints about the inadequacy of benefits matched by complaints about their cost. There has Address for Correspondence: Professor Thomas and Mrs D. WiLron, I Chatford House, The Promenade, CliJon, Eristol, BS83NG. @ Blackwell Publishers Ltd. 1995,108 Cowlg Road, Oxford OX4 lJF, UK and 238 Main Street. Cambridge, MA 02142, USA.

been deepening dissatisfaction, not only in this country but apparently throughout the developed world, with increasing pressure for reform. In Britain, welfare expenditure-here defined as cash benefits, the health and personal social services, education and housing’-rose from just over a fifth of GNP in 1973 to well over a quarter in 1993 ofa GNP that had gone up by more than a third in real terms in the same period. Welfare expenditure had risen by about four-fifths, but “poverty” persists and inequality has increased. The combination of these contrasting facts has strongly suggested the need for another close look at the ways in which resources are being used. The Fowler Review of 1986 made the case for increased selectivity in welfare benefits in order to channel resources to those in greatest need, and the Government, in pursuit of this objective, raised means-tested payments to higher levels than national insurance benefits. A long additional step in this direction is proposed by those commentators who would now abolish the basic retirement pension. However, a move in the opposite direction, back towards social insurance, is one of the recommendations contained in a recent programme for reform-that of the Commission on Social Justice.‘ The Commission was set up in December 1992 at the instigation of the late John Smith, on his becoming leader of the Labour Party. It was given a wide remit to examine “ideas for social reform, economic renewal and political change” over the ensuing decade and to make suggestions about the strategies to be adopted for the implementation of its recommendations. The Commis- sion, under Sir Gordon Borrie, consisted of 15 members of “the great and the good”, drawn from a wide range of academic, political, church, voluntary service, trade-union and business backgrounds. Written and oral evidence was sought from individuals and organizations, and a number of Issue Papers were published as the basis for discussion in the preparation of the Commission’s final report. In this report, the requirements of social justice are “defined in terms of a hierarchy of four ideas. First, the belief that the foundation of a free society is the equal worth of all citizens, expressed most basically in political and civil liberties, equal rights before the law, and so on”-an echo ofRawls here which requires a commitment to a liberal, non-authoritarian society. Second, the argument that “everyone is entitled, as a right ofcitizenship, to be able to meet their basic needs for income, shelter and other necessities”. Third, “ . . . self- respect and equal citizenship demand more than the meeting of basic needs: they demand opportunities and life chances”. It is conceded, fourthly, that “not all inequalities are unjust . . . [but] unjust inequalities should be reduced and where possible eliminated” (17-18). The Report asks whether such a vision ofjustice “can coexist with economic success, or even with economic survival, in a competitive world”. Their answer is that no conflict need occur. On the contrary, “ . . . the economic success of our country requires a greater measure of social justice”. What follows, however, is the astonishing assertion that “ . . . we cannot have social justice without a decent measure of economic success”. Is it really claimed that a poor society, with low GDP per head, cannot be a just society? Justice is about fair shares, not about the total available for sharing out. There seems to be a deep confusion here. Nevertheless, it is encouraging that the Commission has avoided the old 0 Blackwell Publtshers Ltd. 1995 336

mistake of supposing that the reduction of indefensible inequality would by itself free sufficient resources for the many purposes they have in mind. Growth is essential. With its wide remit, the Report naturally covers a wide range of topics: cash benefits, education, health services, housing, community care and envir- onmental issues. In a short section on employment policy the Commission-to its credit-rejects the fashionable idea that unemployment is solely a supply- side problem. Decentralization in government is also considered, but some- what superficially without discussion of the fiscal complications and without mention of the greater danger of lasting single-party domination at lower than at higher levels of government. No reference is made to corruption in local government and no solution is offered for the difficulty of finding enough responsible representatives to man additional tiers of government. This section is much too smooth. Enough has been said to indicate the width of territory covered by the Report. This paper will not attempt to cover so much ground. Attention will be largely confined to what appear to be the basic principles and to the particular way in which these principles are to be applied in one area of policy-that of cash benefits, with special reference to benefits for the elderly. I1 “Building an Intelligent Welfare State” The Commission recommends that the welfare state should be transformed from “a safety net in time of trouble to a springboard for new opportunity”. The emphasis here is partly on the unemployed with larger resources to be devoted to training and re-employment schemes. More generally, there is also to be a radical improvement in education and training for all sections of society. The Commission insists on the need for “ . . . real choices across the life-cycle for men and women in the balance ofemployment, family, education, leisure and retirement”. The nation’s social wealth is to be reconstructed in order to provide what is described as “a dependable social environment in which people can lead their lives” (1-2). The difficulty here is to know what all this would mean in practical terms. The danger is that too much of the available savings would be diverted from the industrial investment on which growth depends. In the case of cash benefits, however, the Report propounds what would appear to be a clear statement of principle: “A new social insurance scheme should be the foundation of long-term reform; although we can never eradicate means-tested benefits com- pletely, the reforms we propose will help restore them to the purpose Beveridge intended-a last resort in time of trouble.” The current system with its reliance on means tests is “fatally flawed” (245). National insurance is to be the centrepiece of the new system-that is to say, more the centrepiece than it is today. The Report contains several statements to this effect, from which it would seem to follow that, apart from residual cases, benefits are to be provided on a “universal basis”, selective by @ Blackwell Publirhers Ltd 1995 337

category-such as age or unemployment-not by individual or family needs. At the same time, the level of benefits is to be raised substantially. It is a bold proposal. An obvious question is how much it would cost, but no estimates are given. These social insurance benefits would have to be sufficient to provide protection against poverty, for “ . . . freedom from poverty for all is at the heart of social justice” (103). Unfortunately, this firm expression of purpose is not followed by any clear explanation of what is meant by “poverty”. Thus the central objective of the whole plan for social security is left strangely vague and ambiguous. It would seem that poverty is most frequently understood in “relative” terms, but there is only one place where a quantitative answer is given, and this without explanation. In Table I .4 on p. 32 of the Report, the poverty level is set at half average (mean) income which is similar to, though not identical with, the EC benchmark of half median earnings. This implies that poverty is entirely relative. No rise, however large, in the standard of living of the “poor”, so defined, will by itself reduce “poverty” for, by definition, it can be reduced only by greater equality. Or in the opposite circumstances, a sharp decline in the average standard of living, caused by, say, some international disaster, would not increase “poverty” unless inequality had been increased. It would have been helpful if the Commission had explained the different senses of the term “poverty” and had given a much-needed warning about the confusing way the term “poverty level” is commonly used to imply a clear and unequivocal meaning. The Report endorses the recommendation of the EC that each member country should declare some level of income to be a minimum income standard “considered sufficient to cover essential needs with regard to respect for human dignity”-a formula which leaves generous scope for differences in interpretation. The Commission also complains that: “ . . . unlike the USA, the government in the United Kingdom does not set a minimum income standard as official indication of the lowest income required for people to be able to stay out of poverty and take part in ordinary social life”. (225) This is really a little hard. It would appear from the Report as a whole that nothing in the British welfare system is remotely satisfactory as compared with what is done in other c~untries.~ It is regrettable that Britain is not given credit at least for having placed so much more emphasis over the years on providing protection against poverty than have most other European countries. For the common European emphasis has been on income replacement by means of benefits related to previous income at work, including incomes far above any conceivable poverty level. It is these cumbersome pension schemes that have added so much to the burden ofsocial security and are leading at last to a more critical assessment of the purpose of compulsory earnings-related contributions for high earnings- related pensions. It is one thing to use compulsion in order to ensure the provision of a reasonable minimum income in old age but quite another matter to impose a state-determined pattern of lifetime consumption. 338 Q Blackwell Publishers Ltd. 1995

The pension guarantee The Borrie Commission would retain the basic retirement pension but would not raise it to the same level as means-tested income support. This is surprising in view of their insistence upon the need to restore social insurance as the centre-piece of social security and in view of their strong condemnation of means-tests as “fatally flawed”. What is termed the “Pension Guarantee” is the principal feature of the Commission’s proposals for the elderly. It is this that will set their minimum income. The amount guaranteed is to be higher than the retirement pension and also above the current level of income support. For an additional payment will be made, determined by personal means in each case. After all that has been said, means-tests are to remain a central feature of the social security system. What is to be changed is the definition of relevant means: (i) by excluding capital, and (ii) by a substantial increase in the amount of other income “disregarded” in assessing L‘needs’’. If it is established that a person has no income apart from the state pension, the difference between that and the guaranteed level will be provided by an additional payment. When, however, there are other sources of income, these will be taken into account. Two possible adjustments are proposed. In the first case, account would be taken only ofany otherpensions, that is to say SERPS or an occupational or personal pension. In the second version, a deduction would also be made for earnings ofover, say, X5,ooo a year and for income from assets of over, say, L500 a year. Capital would, however, be ignored-as in the traditional Australian model. Thus, we are back to “targeting”-not just targeting by category but by personal income. The rhetoric has ended. Selectivity is to be retained but in a weakened form. The traditional side- effects should be made less harmful although, presumably, at higher fiscal cost. For the damage done to the incentives to work and to save should be reduced by excluding capital and by substantially raising the disregards. Another of the familiar criticisms of means-tested benefits has been incomplete take-up, although its importance, in terms of the amount of benefit lost, can easily be exaggerated. This risk should already have been reduced by an administrative change made in 1994 by which all benefits are now available at the same office, or can be obtained through the post. The Commission favours this arrangement, but it would no longer be an innovation because it has been pre-empted by the Conservative G~vernment.~ It is unfortunate that the Commission has made no suggestion, however tentative, about the size of the pension guarantee. Perhaps this omission reflects their failure to indicate what they understand by the “poverty line” at which the pension guarantee might be set. In condemning the current position, the Report is forthright enough, but the standard by which it is judged is sometimes far from clear. Indeed, we find some difficulty in attaching meaning to statements such as “By any measurement, about one-fifth of our population lives in poverty” (32, italics added). One of the most difficult issues is the adjustment of benefits over time. With the current practice of fixing benefits in real terms, their value will fall relative to earnings if real earnings increase. The retirement pension for a married couple, now about 15 per cent ofearnings, will fall to 7f per cent by 2040 on the 0 Blackwell Publishers Ltd. 1995 339

assumption of a rise in real gross earnings of 14 per cent a year. It is true that the rise in real earnings which will reduce the relative value of the pension will also make it easier to save privately against old age, the point usually ignored. Moreover, the 7 i per cent does not allow for SERPS or corresponding contracted-out pensions. The Commission stresses the importance of economic growth, but growth by itselfwill not reduce the relative cost ofbenefits ifthese benefits are linked to earnings. That form of indexation in conjunction with the rising proportion of elderly people and the coming to maturity of SERPS and the effects on the health service of an older population, would together require heavy additional expenditure estimated by John Hills at 5 per cent ofnational income by 2041.5 An extra E5oo million would have to be raised every year on average for these purposes. Hills maintains that this could be done. No doubt it could, but would it be sensible to do so and thus preempt resources on this scale for this particular purpose? What about health services for young people and education and housing? Or is it implicitly assumed that social expenditure will be put up by substantially more than 5 per cent of national income? The Commission is only slightly more cautious than Hills. It proposes that the pension guarantee should be wage-indexed and expresses the hope that the basic pension would be as well, though without a full commitment in this latter case. Thus they are, in effect, recommending a reinstatement of the previous Labour Party promise of wage-indexed pensions. Ifsome formula is really thought to be desirable, there are other possibilities which the Commission might have considered: Pensions could be raised each year by some fraction-say a third-of the rise in earnings in the previous year. When the ageedependency ratio begins to rise once more, an attempt could be made to maintain a roughly constant relationship between the total sum expended on the retirement benefits and aggregate earnings. The average benefit would then decline a little in real terms as compared with average earnings, but the total relative cost of pensions would be held roughly constant, with the average pension increasing in real terms at a little less than real average earnings. The much feared burden ofan ageing population would to this extent be avoided, at least with regard to cash benefits.6 A link could be created, not between pensions and earnings, but between pensions and the rate of return on capital. Under existing arrangements, contributions to national insurance earn entitlement to what is, in effect, an inflation-proofed annuity. Although a valuable component of any retirement income, these contributions do not earn the real rate of return they would earn if invested in indexed bonds. This is where a change might be made. Although unfunded, benefits might be raised by half the rate of return on these bonds in order to reflect the fact that employees contributed about half of total contributions. That is to say, the current rate of increase would be about 1% per cent per annum. Social insurance has lost much of its old character as a contributory-even if never a strictly actuarial-scheme. An arrangement of this kind would indicate that, as in occupational schemes, the contributions made were really 340 @ Blackwell Publishcrs Ltd. 1995

purchasing benefits and not just a component of the general burden of taxation. No commitment to automatic adjustment need, however, be made. It would seem more prudent to rely upon discretionary changes, at least until a better assessment has been made of the other claims on resources. Private pensions The Commission welcomes the growth of private pensions largely, it would seem, in the belief that the tax burden of supporting the elderly can thus be reduced. But what, it must be asked, are the real differences between taxes and contributions to private schemes? There appear to be two. First, a contribu- tion is related to a specific benefit for the contributor in a way in which general taxation is not. Even with social insurance, the link between payments and benefits is rather more blurred than in private schemes. Second, whereas taxes are compulsory, contributions to private schemes need not be so. When compulsion is introduced, as for pensioners contracted out of SERPS, the distinction between contributions and taxation becomes blurred with the implication that compulsory schemes for graduated contributions in return for graduated benefits should not be carried too far.’ The Report contains an interesting discussion of funded pensions and of the choice between minimum-contribution and minimum-benefit schemes. The need for regulation is properly recognized. It seems a pity, however, that no mention is made of the complications for the capital market which would follow from further growth in the already massive pension funds-complica- tions stressed by Titmuss two decades ago.’ Their growth could be a convenient path towards ultimate nationalization-but it is understood that this is not what the present Labour leadership has in mind. The strengths and weaknesses of the report It may be tempting to dismiss the Report as strong on rhetoric but weak on facts and figures. The somewhat regrettable style in which it is written should not, however, be allowed to conceal its merits or to divert attention from some interesting proposals, although usually presented in non-quantitative terms. Thus the pension guarantee deserves careful attention, in particular the case for moving from full means-tests to income-tests and for increasing the disregards. The Commission also suggests that the risk of requiring residential accommodation in old age might be covered by national insurance or by private insurance arrangements assisted by tax concessions. This is now a much discussed possibility. Elsewhere the Commission proposes the adaptation of national insurance in order to meet the needs of part-time workers and the self-employed. Current arrangements are still based on Beveridge’s assumption of full-time employ- ment for the head of the household with a dependent wife not gainfully employed. Largely as a result, “more than three million employees, two-thirds of them women, earn too little to pay contributions. A total of 850,000 self- employed people do not earn themselves any protection for unemployment or 0 Blackwell Pubhsherr Ltd. 1995 34 I

family responsiblities” (229). There is also the problem of temporary and seasonal workers who pay only irregular contributions. This is not to say that these groups are now left unsupported at times of need. All are entitled to income support-a fact not brought out sufficiently in the Report. Social insurance would allow them to escape means-tests but only at the cost of paying the social insurance contribution. The Commission is clearly worried about the burden on low-paid workers and suggests exemption. It may be- though the exposition is far from clear-that they would have low-earners, including part-timers, receive social insurance benefits without either income- tests or contribution records. On balance, would the part-timers really benefit? Against any possible advantage of being insured must also be set the effect on employment. At present part-time employment is subsidised by the taxpayer because the means-tested social benefits that such workers may claim are financed from general taxation. If brought into social insurance, contributions would have to be made by the employers as well as employees, and labour costs would thus be raised with employment prospects probably damaged. Against any such disadvantage must be set the removal of the current incentive to employers to replace full-time with part-time workers when this is possible. 111 The Missing Plan for Social Expenditure The proposals we have discussed above are some examples of the many put forward in this wide-ranging Report. The Report fails, however, to present a coherent plan for action. It is a compendium ofwhat are believed to be socially desirable projects but these projects compete with one another as well as with private claims on resources. Estimates of probable cost, even if tentative, would have given more shape and form to their proposals, but are missing from the Report. For the Labour Party to endorse their recommendations would therefore be a leap in the dark. The Commission seeks to defend this lack of estimates by saying that they are looking ahead for about fifteen years, which makes forecasting even more difficult than for the life of a single parliament. However, some illumination could surely have been provided by giving rough estimates at least for the first five years. After all Beveridge attempted, even in wartime, to determine some probable orders of magnitude which were by no means useless in assessing his proposals. By comparison, the Borrie Commission could have drawn upon an enormous mass ofaccumulated research findings and could have engaged the services of modern experts armed with modern technology rather than slide rules! There can be no serious doubt that the full range of their recommendations would be costly. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has in fact estimated the cost of some of the main proposals at C7 b i l l i ~ n . ~ Not only would the cash benefits cost more but large sums would be required for the improvements also proposed in education and in the health and other services. There are also vaguely described, but probably large, improvements to be made in social capital-competing for savings with the large increase in industrial investment on which great emphasis has been placed by the Labour Party’s leadership. It need not, of course, be assumed that lower taxation takes precedence over all other 342 0 Blackwell Publishers Ltd. 1995

objectives in the public mind. As the Commission notes, the British Social Attitudes Survey has reported that “the majority say they would prefer both taxes and spending to increase”.’O This is an interesting pointer but we still need to know how much more taxation for how much more improvement in public services would be acceptable. Unfortunately the Commission’s emphasis on the need for a growing economy, however desirable in other ways, can allow growth to become a panacea. When there is any suspicion of conflict between desirable objectives, growth can be called upon to provide the solution. Many governments in the past have tried valiantly to achieve faster growth in Britain and have done so not wholly without success. There may be further success in the future, but it can never be on such a scafe as to remove the competition between different claims, both public and private. The Commission would have done well to draw attention to the massive increases in the past in public expenditure on social welfare as a percentage ofsubstantially increased GNP. For example, as noted in a recent parliamentary report, real expenditure on cash benefits alone has risen by 700 per cent between 1g4g/50 and 199213. Yet these benefits are still said to be sadly inadequate. The NHS, education, housing-any service one cares to name-is held to be “underfunded”. Of course there are further improvements that can and should be made. That is not in doubt. But “underfunding” will remain a chronic complaint because the demands made will never be satisfied. The Labour Party seems to have largely abandoned its former belief in industrial planning and this may be fortunate. But any government-Left or Right-needs a plan for its own public expenditure that will allow each of the various claims on resources to be properly assessed in its proper context. A plan of this kind might usefully include a maximum for social expenditure -reasonably defined-as a percentage of national income. In practice, the prescribed limit might sometimes be exceeded-and for reasons that could not be excused as cyclical. Even so, the ceiling would at least serve as a warning and as a reply to persistent complaints about underfunding. Moreover, a ceiling of this kind would help to bring home the fact that different parts of the social budget are in competition with one another. Unfortunately, the Commission offers not even the outline of such a plan. However stimulating, its report is no more than a preliminary commentary before the real work begins. Any radical change in the provision of public services is also bound to entail transitional costs. Large changes have already been carried out in recent years in social security, in the health service, in the personal social services, in education, in housing and in local government. As well as the additional cost in public administration, there is the penalty imposed on private people when what appeared to be reasonable expectations are upset. For this reason, a period of consolidation would now be beneficial but is not to be expected, for there is too much continuing dissatisfaction, even more perhaps on the part of politicians and professionals than on the part of the general public. It is, however, much to be hoped that when further changes come to be made, some weight will be given to the desirability of ensuring that the innovations are generally acceptable and therefore have some chance of being durable. Reform @ Blackwell Publishers Ltd. 1995 343

indeed, but reform followed by reasonable stability. That ought surely to be the objective ofany future government, but it will not be achieved until there is a wider and more coherent consensus about the objectives the welfare state is designed to serve and the cost their achievement would necessarily entail.
